Title: DeepImagine: Learning Biomedical Reasoning via Successive Counterfactual Imagining

DeepImagine: Learning Biomedical Reasoning via
Successive Counterfactual Imagining

Abstract
Predicting the outcomes of prospective clinical trials remains a major challenge
for large language models (LLMs). Prior work has shown that both traditional
correlational predictors, such as random forests and logistic regression, and strong
commercial LLMs achieve limited performance on this task. In this paper, we pro-
pose DeepImagine, a framework for teaching LLMs biomedical reasoning through
successive counterfactual imagining. The central idea is to approximate hidden
causal mechanisms of clinical trials by training models to infer how observed trial
results would change under controlled perturbations of experimental conditions,
such as dosage, outcome measures, study arms, geography, and other trial attributes.
To support this objective, we construct both natural and approximate counterfac-
tual pairs from real clinical trials with reported outcomes. For settings where
strict counterfactual supervision is available, such as paired outcome measures or
dose-ranging study arms within the same trial, we train models with supervised
fine-tuning. For broader settings where only approximate counterfactual pairs
can be retrieved, we optimize models with reinforcement learning using verifiable
rewards based on downstream benchmark correctness. We further augment training
with synthetic reasoning traces that provide causally plausible explanations for
local counterfactual transitions. Using this pipeline, we train language models
under 10B parameters, including Qwen3.5-9B, and evaluate them on clinical trial
outcome prediction. We aim to show that DeepImagine consistently improves over
untuned language models and traditional correlational baselines. Finally, we aim
to show that the learned reasoning trajectories provide interpretable signals about
how models represent trial-level mechanisms, suggesting a practical path toward
more mechanistic and scientifically useful biomedical language models.

Introduction
Clinical trial outcomes are influenced by a wide range of factors. Some of these are relatively
observable, including enrollment size, trial phase, location, and sponsor characteristics. Larger
enrollment can increase statistical power, making it easier to detect statistically significant effects.
Phase III trials often face a higher threshold for success, as they represent one of the final stages
before a drug can receive FDA approval. Trial location may also matter, since studies conducted
in developed countries may benefit from stronger procedural adherence and tighter control over
participants than those conducted in developing countries. Sponsor characteristics can further shape

outcomes, as larger companies often have greater resources, more experienced research teams, and
more mature development pipelines than small or mid-sized firms.
Despite the importance of these factors, it remains difficult to formulate an exact equation that
specifies how they interact and jointly determine the outcome of a clinical trial. In addition, many non-
clinical external factors may also affect trial results, although such factors are outside the scope of this
work. Still, we hypothesize that clinical trial outcomes are ultimately governed by underlying laws
and mechanisms, possibly with some degree of randomness, which means that there should exist a
hidden set of causal laws and mechanisms that determines how these factors jointly produce observed
results. If such laws and mechanisms could be identified, they could enable highly accurate prediction
of trial outcomes. In this paper, we refer to this latent set of governing laws and mechanisms as the
hidden causal model of clinical trial outcomes.
The central insight of this paper is that LLMs can improve prediction of a prospective clinical trial
when the target trial can be linked to many highly similar historical trials with reported outcomes,
and when the model is allowed to condition on those prior results. Although the success of a previous
trial does not guarantee the success of a new one, we find that trials associated with a larger fraction
of successful predecessors tend to have a higher probability of success. Conventional correlational
methods would typically encode this signal as a numerical feature, such as the proportion of related
prior trials that succeeded. In contrast, we hypothesize that an LLM can use these prior trials
more mechanistically, by reasoning through a sequence of counterfactual imaginations. Specifically,
beginning with a historical trial whose outcome is known, we change one experimental condition at
a time to match the target trial, keeping all remaining conditions fixed, and ask the model to infer
how the known outcome would change under that perturbation. By repeating this process over all
differing factors, the model effectively traverses a chain of counterfactual states from the historical
trial to the target trial, and the final imagined outcome becomes the prediction. See Figure 1 for an
example of successive counterfactual imagination.
In this paper, we propose a training method that enables LLMs to gradually internalize these governing
mechanisms. Our approach trains models on coupled experiments, where all experimental conditions
are kept fixed except for a single factor. For instance, we provide a sequence of experiments with
identical patient demographics, intervention drugs, locations, study designs, and outcome measures,
while varying only the dosage from 10 mg daily to 100 mg daily. Importantly, each experiment in
this sequence is drawn from a real clinical study with reported results. As a result, although the
experiments function as counterfactual variants of one another for training purposes, they are all
grounded in real-world outcomes. We train the model via supervised fine-tuning using these data.
For many variables, corresponding counterfactuals are unavailable. In this work, we use the term
counterfactual to refer to a pair of clinical trial experiments in which only one condition differs while
all other conditions are held fixed. In practice, this type of strict counterfactual is rarely available,
because it would require a real clinical trial to have been conducted under an alternative version of
the same experimental setup, with every aspect unchanged except for the single variable of interest.
Consequently, although such counterfactual settings can be easily imagined, their true outcomes are
usually unobservable. To address this limitation, we develop an information retrieval pipeline that
links clinical trials with highly similar experimental settings, enabling the construction of approximate
counterfactual pairs grounded in real reported outcomes. Empirically, we find that these pairings
often differ in only a small number of variables. For example, a company may conduct a successful
Phase II trial and subsequently launch a Phase III trial for the same drug. Although both trials involve
the same intervention, they may differ in success criteria, such as outcome measures, and the Phase
III trial may enroll a larger and more heterogeneous patient population. Using such pairings, we
train the model to discover its own reasoning traces, rewarding it solely for its ability to predict the
outcome of one trial from the other to a meaningful degree.
Taken together, these ideas suggest a different role for language models in clinical trial prediction:
rather than acting purely as correlational predictors, they can be trained to approximate the latent
causal mechanisms that govern how trial outcomes change under controlled perturbations of experi-
mental conditions. Building on this view, we introduce DeepImagine, a framework that combines
natural and approximate counterfactual trial pairings, synthetic causal reasoning traces, and reinforce-
ment learning over verifiable outcomes. Through this combination, we aim to teach LLMs to perform
successive counterfactual imagination as a practical approximation to biomedical causal reasoning.
Empirically, we show that this approach improves prospective clinical trial outcome prediction over

Related Work
Causal Inference:
Our work is grounded in the structural causal model (SCM) view of causality,
where causal questions are framed in terms of interventions and counterfactuals rather than correla-
tions [19]. In particular, Pearl’s abduction–action–prediction formulation motivates our notion of
successive counterfactual imagining. Unlike classical causal inference, however, we do not assume
access to a fully specified SCM for clinical trials; instead, we train a language model to approximate
counterfactual transitions from real and approximate trial pairs.
Causal LLM and Techniques to Train Them:
Recent work has examined whether LLMs can
perform causal reasoning reliably. Kıcıman et al. [11] show that strong LLMs can often produce
plausible causal arguments but remain brittle. Jin et al. [10] introduced CLadder and showed that
formally grounded causal reasoning remains difficult for current models. Related benchmarks extend
this direction: ExpliCa evaluates explicit causal and temporal reasoning [15], CounterBench studies
formal counterfactual inference [3], and executable counterfactual work argues that many settings
overestimate counterfactual ability by bypassing abduction [24]. At the training level, process
supervision has been shown to improve multi-step reasoning relative to pure outcome supervision
[14]. Our work builds on these ideas but focuses on biomedical forecasting, where LLMs reason over
linked clinical trials rather than abstract causal tasks.
Clinical Trial Benchmarks:
Clinical trial outcome prediction has been studied through both
specialized models and benchmark frameworks. HINT uses multimodal trial representations for
outcome prediction [4], while SPOT models sequential relations among similar historical trials [31].
PyTrial provides a broader framework for machine learning on clinical-trial tasks, including outcome
prediction and similarity search [30]. On the data side, CTO offers a large-scale clinical trial outcome
resource [6], while CT Open introduces an open, time-stamped, decontaminated benchmark for
prospective outcome prediction [28]. Our work is most closely aligned with CT Open because
we focus on prospective, uncontaminated evaluation. Our retrieval component is also related to
Trial2Vec [29], though we use similar trials not only for retrieval but also as anchors for successive
counterfactual imagination.
3


Reinforcement Learning:
Our reinforcement-learning stage builds on policy optimization and
RL-for-LLM training. PPO introduced the clipped surrogate objective that remains a standard method
for stable policy optimization [20]. In language modeling, reinforcement learning from feedback
was popularized by work on summarization with human feedback [22] and InstructGPT [18]. More
recently, DeepSeekMath proposed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which removes the
separate critic and uses group-relative rewards for more memory-efficient reasoning-oriented training
[21]. We adopt GRPO in a different regime, where the model receives reward only for terminal
correctness in clinical trial prediction and must discover useful latent counterfactual trajectories.
Synthetic Data Generation:
Synthetic data generation has been widely used for retrieval and
question answering when labeled supervision is limited. IR2 studies synthetic-query generation for
retrieval under low-resource settings [25], while single-pass document scanning make an innovative
use of linked data to make synthetic data to teach model the ability of long-range reasoning [1]. Other
work improves diversity and task alignment through retrieved or transformed supervision, including
DataTune [5] and Genie [32]. Synthetic data has also been used to build compositional supervision
for multi-hop QA [2]. Our setting differs in that we generate supervision for counterfactual transitions
between highly similar clinical trials rather than standalone QA pairs, while aligning to the critical
insight in [1] that shows pairing existing data in new ways could teach model new skills.
Biomedical Reasoning:
Biomedical reasoning has been evaluated through both broad NLP bench-
marks and specialized evidence-centric tasks. BLURB provides a general biomedical benchmark suite
[8], while PubMedQA and BioASQ-QA evaluate literature-grounded biomedical question answering
[9, 12]. More recent benchmarks target higher-level scientific reasoning: EvidenceBench evaluates
evidence retrieval and synthesis for biomedical hypotheses [27], and RoBBR measures risk-of-bias
estimation in biomedical studies [26]. These tasks align with the broader tradition of evidence-based
biomedical reasoning and critical appraisal [7]. In contrast, we study whether LLMs can use linked
historical trials to perform successive counterfactual imagination for prospective clinical trial outcome
prediction.
3
Preliminary
3.1
Counterfactual Imagining in Causal Inference
In causal inference, counterfactual reasoning asks what would have happened to an outcome had
some aspect of the world been different, while all other causally relevant mechanisms remained
governed by the same underlying system. In the structural causal model (SCM) framework of Pearl,
a causal model is typically written as
M = (U, V, F, P(U)),
where U denotes exogenous variables, V denotes endogenous variables, F is a collection of struc-
tural assignments, and P(U) specifies the distribution over background factors. An intervention
do(X = x) replaces the structural equation for X with the assignment X = x, thereby defining a
modified submodel in which the downstream consequences of that intervention can be evaluated.
Counterfactual quantities are then written as expressions such as Yx, denoting the value that Y would
attain under the intervention do(X = x), and more generally as conditional probabilities of the form
P(Yx = y | e),
where e denotes factual evidence about the realized world.
A standard account of counterfactual evaluation in Pearl’s framework proceeds in three steps: ab-
duction, action, and prediction. In the abduction step, the model updates its beliefs about latent
background variables using the observed evidence e. In the action step, it modifies the model by
imposing the hypothetical intervention do(X = x). In the prediction step, it computes the resulting
outcome in the modified model. Thus, counterfactual inference is not merely prediction under a new
input; rather, it is prediction for the same underlying unit after minimally altering the relevant causal
mechanism specified by the antecedent. This distinction is important because counterfactuals inherit
information from the factual world through abduction before the hypothetical change is applied.
Motivated by this tradition, we use the term counterfactual imagining to denote a model-side ap-
proximation to counterfactual inference: starting from an observed clinical trial result, the model
4


imagines how that result would change if one trial condition were perturbed while all other relevant
conditions were held fixed. Formally, if x(0) denotes a source trial configuration with observed result
R(0), and x(T ) denotes a target configuration, then a successive counterfactual imagination procedure
constructs a path
x(0), x(1), . . . , x(T ),
where each consecutive pair differs in exactly one experimental condition. The model then generates
a corresponding sequence
R(1), R(2), . . . , R(T ),
with each R(t) interpreted as the imagined result obtained after applying a local perturbation from
x(t−1) to x(t). In this sense, our formulation can be viewed as a sequential approximation to a
complex counterfactual query: instead of directly estimating the target result from scratch, the model
traverses a chain of local “what-if” transformations from the observed source trial to the unobserved
target trial.
Our use of counterfactual imagining is therefore inspired by, but not identical to, classical SCM-based
counterfactual inference. In the ideal SCM formulation, a counterfactual such as
P(Rx′ | e)
is defined with respect to a fully specified causal model and evaluated through abduction, action,
and prediction. In our setting, the true causal law is unknown and only partial supervision is
available. We therefore train a language model Pθ to approximate this process through successive
local transformations, using observed source results as factual evidence and trial-pair differences
as approximate interventions. The goal is not to claim access to the full SCM of clinical trials, but
rather to induce a practically useful approximation to counterfactual reasoning that preserves the
central Pearlian intuition: infer what would happen under a hypothetical change by anchoring the
computation in what is already known about the factual case.
3.2
Clinical Trial Terminology
We first give a quick introduction to terminology used in clinical trial outcome prediction, following
the convention of CT Open.
Definition (Intervention/Treatment). For clinical trials, an intervention, or treatment, refers to the
therapeutic regimen being evaluated. This may consist of a single drug, a combination of drugs,
a medical procedure, or a combination of drugs and procedures. Example: A trial evaluating
pembrolizumab alone, or pembrolizumab combined with chemotherapy, would treat these regimens
as interventions.
Definition (Study, Treatment, and Comparator Arms). A study arm is a group of participants assigned
to a particular condition within a clinical trial. A treatment arm receives the intervention being tested,
whereas a comparator arm serves as the control condition, such as a placebo, standard of care, or
another treatment. Example: In a two-arm trial, one group may receive a new cancer drug, while the
comparator arm receives standard chemotherapy.
Definition (Outcome Measure and Endpoint). An outcome measure, also called an endpoint, is a
pre-specified quantity used to evaluate the effect of an intervention in a clinical trial. It defines what
will be measured and is part of the trial design, rather than the observed trial result. Example: The
5-year overall survival rate is an outcome measure.
Definition (Result and Outcome). A result, or outcome, is the observed value of an outcome measure
after the trial has been conducted. It describes what actually happened in the trial. Example: “85%
of patients survived for at least 5 years after treatment” is a result, whereas “5-year overall survival
rate” is the corresponding outcome measure.
We formally define a unit of results, given a clinical trial Ci1, one of its proposed outcome measure
Oj1, and a study arm (i.e. a group that receives a specific kind of intervention) Ak1, the reported
results is defined as RCi1,Oj1,Ak1. Intuitively speaking, our goal is to transform RCi1,Oj1,Ak1
to RCi2,Oj2,Ak2 via our trained language models’ successive counterfactual imaginations. Note,
RCi2,Oj2,Ak2 represents the results for another clinical trial Ci2, its proposed outcome measure Oj2,
and its study arm Ak2.

Interpretation.
Importantly, our formulation does not claim that the true law itself is sequential.
Rather, the sequential decomposition is an approximation strategy for the learned model. The
true data-generating law P is assumed to depend only on the current experimental condition x(t),
whereas the learned model Pθ is trained to approximate this law through a sequence of simpler local
counterfactual updates.
4.1
Discovering Natural Counterfactuals
In practice, a clinical trial often includes multiple outcome measures and multiple study arms. On
average, a trial contains roughly two primary outcome measures and eight to ten secondary outcome
measures, reflecting the fact that clinical studies are typically designed to evaluate several aspects of
an intervention rather than a single effect. Controlled trials contain at least two arms: a comparator
arm, often placebo or standard of care, and an intervention arm. In many cases, however, a trial
includes more than two arms. Beyond the baseline comparator arm, there may be multiple treatment
arms, each corresponding to a different intervention regimen. For example, one arm may administer
10 mg of a drug per day, another 20 mg per day, and a third 30 mg per day. This type of design is
commonly referred to as a dose-ranging or dosing study, in which investigators seek to determine
whether treatment effects become more pronounced as dosage increases.

4.2
Approximating Other Counterfactuals
For all remaining variables, we absorb them into the clinical trial symbol C. These variables include,
among others, the drug’s biological mechanism of action, geography (i.e., the countries in which
participating hospitals administer the intervention), and patient eligibility criteria, whose inclusion
and exclusion rules jointly define the health profile of the enrolled population. In general, natural
counterfactuals for these variables are difficult to obtain. Nevertheless, a few important exceptions
do arise in practice. First, the baseline comparator is sometimes not a placebo but an established
drug. In such cases, the comparator and the investigational drug often share certain similarities
while still differing in clinically meaningful ways. These pairings may therefore encourage the
model to internally represent how trial results change when the intervention drug changes while other
aspects of the trial remain similar. Second, a clinical trial conducted in a single country may later
motivate a follow-up trial with an otherwise similar design but expanded to multiple countries or
conducted globally. Such pairings provide a natural counterfactual setting for studying how changes
in geography affect trial outcomes.
Outside these special cases, natural counterfactuals rarely exist for most trial variables. We therefore
construct approximate counterfactual pairs using a combination of LLM-based information retrieval
and FDA drug monographs. For each retrieved pair of trials, Ci1 and Ci2, the corresponding trial
attributes are highly similar overall, but several variables may differ simultaneously. In this setting, it
is no longer feasible to construct supervision signals for a full sequence of one-variable perturbations,
since the intermediate counterfactual outcomes are not observed in reality. Nevertheless, we retain
the same hypothesis as in the supervised setting: successive counterfactual imagination remains
the easier inductive path for the model. Rather than predicting the target result R(T ) directly from
x(T ), the model begins from the known source result R(0) and generates a latent sequence of local
counterfactual transitions that gradually transforms x(0) into x(T ).
Because these intermediate counterfactual states are unobserved, we can no longer optimize the
model with direct stepwise supervision. Instead, we optimize Pθ with reinforcement learning using

The model is never directly supervised on the intermediate states R(1), . . . , R(T −1); instead, these
states remain latent. Reinforcement learning encourages Pθ to discover intermediate counterfactual
trajectories whose local transitions are plausible enough that the final imagined target result R(T )
yields the correct verifiable answer. In this sense, GRPO optimizes the same sequential counterfactual
mechanism introduced earlier, but under terminal supervision rather than stepwise supervision.
9


4.3
Synthetic Reasoning for Supervised Fine-tuning
Empirically, during each turn in our successive counterfactual imagination, we add a synthetic
reasoning trace that gives a plausibly causal explanation of why changing x(t−1) into x(t) would
cause R(t−1) to change into R(t), this reasoning is produced by a powerful GPT5.4 that has full
access to both x(t−1), x(t) and R(t−1), R(t). This reasoning is validated by our biomedical experts
as being plausible. While the true data generating law remains hidden, we would have no way to
actually verifying the correctness of such synthetic reasoning traces. In our experiments, we have
found our language model fine-tuned on such synthetic reasoning traces would produce considerable
improvements in terms of accurately predicting a single step of counterfactual imagining, as well
as GPT5.4 can do, without going through GRPO. We denote the synthetic reasoning trace as
W = (w0, w1, . . . , wn) where each wi is a token. Thus the formulation is turned into.
Pθ(W, R(t) | R(t−1), x(t−1), x(t))

5
Experiment Setup
5.1
Evaluation Dataset Construction
We evaluate our approach by its downstream utility for clinical trial outcome prediction. From the
training split of [28], we draw 250 random questions from each of the Superiority and Comparative
Effect classes of the clinical trial outcome prediction task.
To further assess the quality of the two counterfactual perturbation independently, we construct two
dedicated evaluation datasets from this sample:
Outcome-measure perturbation set.
For each (trial, outcome measure) pair in the evaluation
sample, we identify the most similar alternative outcome measure within the same trial, ranked by
cosine similarity of the embeddings from [13]. A evaluated model is provided with the reported result
of the nearest outcome measure and asked to predict the target outcome measure’s result under the
same study arm.
Study-arm perturbation set.
Each evaluation question is associated with two study arms reported
under a common outcome measure. We fix one of these arms and pair it with a different study arm
drawn from the same trial that was measured under the same outcome. A evaluated model is provided
with the paired arm’s reported result and asked to predict the fixed arm’s result.
5.2
Model Fine-Tuning
Following the methodology in §4.1, we use gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 [17], with medium reasoning
effort and low verbosity, to generate synthetic counterfactual reasoning trajectories for study-arm
and outcome-measure perturbations, giving about 26k trajectories for each perturbation type. We
fine-tuned Qwen-3.5-9B [23] with LoRA on each of the arm-perturbation and outcome-measure
perturbation sets. LoRA adapters were applied to all linear layers with rank r = 32, scaling factor
α = 64, and dropout 0.05. We trained for one epoch with a per-device batch size of 1 and gradient
accumulation of 2. Optimization used AdamW with a peak learning rate of 5 × 10−5, cosine decay to
a minimum 0.1 of the peak learning rate, 5% warm-up steps, zero weight decay, and gradient clipping
at 1.0. The maximum sequence length was 8,192 tokens. Training was performed on a single node
with 7x80GB H100 GPUs using FlashAttention-4. See Table 1 for detailed training hyperparameter
settings. See Figure 2 for training loss curve.

7
Conclusion
In this work, we introduced DeepImagine, a framework for teaching language models biomedical
reasoning through successive counterfactual imagining. Our central premise is that, although the
true causal laws governing clinical trial outcomes remain hidden, highly similar historical trials with
reported results can provide useful anchors for approximating how outcomes change under controlled
perturbations of trial conditions. By combining natural counterfactual supervision, approximate
counterfactual retrieval, synthetic reasoning traces, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards,
we train language models to predict prospective clinical trial outcomes through sequences of local
counterfactual transitions rather than one-shot correlational prediction. Empirically, this approach
improves performance over conventional correlational baselines and untuned language models,
while also yielding interpretable reasoning traces that can be analyzed to recover structured causal
hypotheses. More broadly, our results suggest that counterfactual imagination may provide a practical
path toward more mechanistic and scientifically useful reasoning in biomedical language models.

Abstract: Predicting the outcomes of prospective clinical trials remains a major challenge for large language models (LLMs). Prior work has shown that both traditional correlational predictors, such as random forests and logistic regression, and strong commercial LLMs achieve limited performance on this task. In this paper, we pro- pose DeepImagine, a framework for teaching LLMs biomedical reasoning through successive counterfactual imagining. The central idea is to approximate hidden causal mechanisms of clinical trials by training models to infer how observed trial results would change under controlled perturbations of experimental conditions, such as dosage, outcome measures, study arms, geography, and other trial attributes. To support this objective, we construct both natural and approximate counterfac- tual pairs from real clinical trials with reported outcomes. For settings where strict counterfactual supervision is available, such as paired outcome measures or dose-ranging study arms within the same trial, we train models with supervised fine-tuning. For broader settings where only approximate counterfactual pairs can be retrieved, we optimize models with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards based on downstream benchmark correctness. We further augment training with synthetic reasoning traces that provide causally plausible explanations for local counterfactual transitions. Using this pipeline, we train language models under 10B parameters, including Qwen3.5-9B, and evaluate them on clinical trial outcome prediction. We aim to show that DeepImagine consistently improves over untuned language models and traditional correlational baselines. Finally, we aim to show that the learned reasoning trajectories provide interpretable signals about how models represent trial-level mechanisms, suggesting a practical path toward more mechanistic and scientifically useful biomedical language models.
